newsitem.title: FINLAND: Helsinki set to replay key role in east-west ties.
newsitem.headline: Helsinki set to replay key role in east-west ties.

text.p: Venue for many key east-west summits in the Cold War, the Finnish capital, conveniently close to Moscow and steadfastly non-aligned, is set to be the site for another high-profile U.S.-Russian encounter.

Helsinki's wind-swept granite boulevards offer classic territory for a summit next month between U.S. President Bill Clinton and Russia's Boris Yeltsin, who has health problems and will be only one and a half hours from Moscow by air.

"We are very optimistic about the success of the summit, since Finland has an almost traditional preparedness to arrange meetings like this," Finnish Foreign Minister Tarja Halonen told a news conference.

The key issue the two leaders will discuss -- the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation's plans to expand, which Russia fiercely opposes -- is an area where Finland has no direct interest as it is not an alliance member.
Its defence policy spurns NATO membership, but today cites "independence" rather than "neutrality" as laid down in a defunct 1948 agreement with the former Soviet Union.
In its past role as a west-facing country with a long border with the Soviet Union, Helsinki's solid, pastel buildings have witnessed many meetings between East and West.
City-dwellers talk of the "Helsinki spirit" as fostering closer ties between sometimes hostile powers.
Key meetings in Helsinki's history include:
* In 1969, the SALT nuclear arms reduction talks took place here.
* In 1975, U.S. President Gerald Ford, Communist Party Secretary Leonid Brezhnev and 33 other heads of state attended a reception here to celebrate the historic Helsinki Final Act.
* In 1990 Clinton's predecessor George Bush and the Soviet Union's Mikhail Gorbachev met here.
* In February 1996, Russian foreign minister Yevgeny Primakov and former U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher met for the first time here.

The 1975 meeting in particular is held up by some observers as heralding the beginning of the end of the Soviet Union. It sealed Europe's post-war borders, but also made the former Soviet dictatorship commit itself to respecting human rights.
Ford has since called the Helsinki Act "a Trojan Horse for Liberty behind the iron curtain".
Once the capital of the Grand Duchy of Finland under the Russian empire, the greater Helsinki area is home to 900,000 and holds many reminders of Moscow's past glory.
During the Cold War Finland's leaders maintained a special relationship with their Kremlin counterparts, and were careful to respect Moscow's foreign policy interests.
Soviet state founder Vladimir Lenin is seen as the bestower of independence to Finland in 1917, after hiding out in the country several times while planning his revolution.
But Finland in 1995 took its most decisive step west, joining the European Union, and now Helsinki has a thoroughly western air.
A short walk through the city takes the visitor past Paris-style cafes on roads meticulously cleared of snow, where fur-coated shoppers chat on designer mobile-phones.
As well as a clutch of famed Russian restaurants and a beer called Sinebrychoff, there is Skippy peanut butter and live TV screening of the Superbowl.
The U.S. President's wife Hillary Rodham Clinton has already been to Helsinki -- although her visit last July did not involve high-level political talks.
